method: TWO SOURCES OF DIFFERENT KIND. A1 is the Australian Medicines Handbook therapeutic topic 'Acne' (July 2026 release), read under the subscription on this machine and PARAPHRASED. No AMH passage is reproduced and no source_text is stored, because storing it would redistribute licensed content; each A1 claim carries a locator naming the topic and retrieval date and has verdict licensed_source_not_quoted. Those claims CANNOT be machine re-checked from this repository and must be verified against a subscription. No citation has been attached to an A1 claim from any other work: a claim read in AMH and cited to a paper located afterwards would record a provenance that did not happen, and the verbatim check would pass while the attribution was false. S2 is open access, fetched with curl, and every S2 claim is verbatim-checked with scripts/verify.py. AMH drug monograph doses were deliberately not transcribed.

claims.claim: Acne vulgaris arises from increased sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinisation, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes and inflammation, and management is directed at these factors
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Mild acne is mainly comedones with some papules and pustules; moderate is more widespread papules and pustules with possible mild scarring; severe has nodules, pseudocysts and widespread papules and pustules with possible extensive scarring
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Treatment should start early to prevent scarring and be tailored to severity
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Stated aims of drug treatment include improving complexion, preventing scarring, limiting disease duration and reducing acne-related depression and low self esteem
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Doxycycline is contraindicated after 18 weeks gestation, equivalent to 16 weeks post conception, but is safe before that point
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Isotretinoin is used for severe acne and for moderate acne unresponsive to first-line treatment
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Oral hormonal treatment may be added in females with moderate or severe acne
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Topical retinoids are the treatment of choice for both comedonal and inflammatory acne and may be combined with other topical and oral treatments, but irritation may increase when more than one topical is used
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Topical retinoids are not to be used in pregnancy because of teratogenic risk
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide is antibacterial and mildly comedolytic, useful in comedonal and mild inflammatory acne
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Azelaic acid is antibacterial and comedolytic and is a less irritating alternative to benzoyl peroxide in mild inflammatory acne
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Azelaic acid should be used cautiously in patients with dark complexions because it may cause hypopigmentation, although that effect may be useful where acne has left hyperpigmented scars
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Topical clindamycin should be changed if there is no response after 6 to 8 weeks, stopped once inflammatory lesions resolve adequately, and limited to 3 months where possible
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Oral antibacterials should be combined with a topical retinoid and either benzoyl peroxide or azelaic acid, changed if there is no response after 6 to 8 weeks, and limited to 3 to 6 months when possible
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, therapeutic topic 'Acne' (Dermatological drugs > Drugs for acne), July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Antibacterials should not be switched or rotated in a patient who is responding, because response indicates efficacy and changing agents may promote resistance

claims.claim: Oral hormonal treatments are limited to females and reduce sebum secretion, which is under androgen control; several months are usually required before benefit appears and prolonged treatment is needed to maintain it

claims.claim: A combined oral contraceptive may be added to a topical retinoid, benzoyl peroxide or azelaic acid in moderate acne, either in addition to or instead of an oral antibacterial

claims.claim: Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation is a common complication of acne in skin of colour and should not be ignored
claims.source_text: which is a common complication of acne in patients with skin of colour. It should not be ignored

claims.claim: General measures first: SPF 50+ sunscreen, protective clothing and avoiding irritation
claims.source_text: Because the patient is yet to trial any therapies, general measures should be suggested first. Photoprotection through the use of broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 50+) and protective clothing, such as hats, will reduce further darkening of the affected skin. Avoiding skin irritation, such as from scratching, rubbing or irritating fragrant skincare products, is also important

claims.claim: The acne must be treated to treat the hyperpigmentation
claims.source_text: However, to best treat the PIH, the acne must also be treated

claims.claim: Occlusive hair oils and pomades contribute to acne and should be addressed culturally sensitively
claims.source_text: The patient should be educated on how the use of occlusive hair oils and pomades contributed to her acne and encouraged, in a culturally sensitive way, to stop using these products

claims.claim: Practical alternatives to oil-based hair products and an application distance if they are retained
claims.source_text: An example of a culturally sensitive approach would be to try to learn about the hair care practices for this patient and to provide alternatives to oil-based products, such as silicone, along with practical recommendations for washing her hair weekly or fortnightly with clarifying shampoo … she could consider application 2-3 cm away from the hairline with a covering over the hair at night to prevent indirect spread to the skin

claims.claim: Tretinoin and adapalene are the commonly prescribed Australian retinoids and should be introduced at low concentration a few times weekly
claims.source_text: Topical tretinoin and adapalene are commonly prescribed retinoids in Australia for both acne and PIH. Due to the irritant potential of all retinoids, low concentrations should be used initially, with application starting a few times per week and gradually increasing as tolerated

claims.claim: Escalation to oral antibiotics at about eight weeks, and isotretinoin for severe unresponsive cases
claims.source_text: If the acne does not demonstrate improvement over a period of approximately eight weeks, oral antibiotics could be considered. Oral isotretinoin (dermatologist referral needed) might be required for severe cases that are not responsive to topical therapy alone and in which triggers are unable to be completely eliminated

claims.claim: Additional PIH treatments include hydroquinone, azelaic acid, chemical peels and laser
claims.source_text: These include topical hydroquinone, azelaic acid, chemical peels and laser-based treatments

claims.claim: Hydroquinone is applied to the whole face rather than as spot treatment
claims.source_text: Application to the entire face is preferred over spot treatment for multiple areas of involvement to prevent irregular pigmentation
